title: Derandomizing the Exact Matching problem
short_statement: Find a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Exact Matching, the problem of deciding whether a graph has a perfect matching with exactly $k$ red edges.
open_problem: Find a verified deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for Exact Matching on arbitrary graphs. A 2026 bipartite claim is recorded below with a concrete issue in a subsidiary statement; it does not settle the general-graph problem.
background: Exact Matching is a deceptively small extension of ordinary perfect matching. Ordinary matching is one of the central polynomial-time problems in combinatorial optimization, but adding the exact cardinality constraint on one color class moves the known general algorithmic status into randomized polynomial time. The problem also appears as a hardness core inside robust and recoverable assignment models, so it is not just a complexity-theory curiosity. The randomized algorithm of Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani is based on algebraic isolation: assign random weights so that a relevant matching is isolated with good probability, then use determinant or Pfaffian computations. Derandomizing this step is a long-standing open problem connected to the broader project of derandomizing isolation lemmas. Recent deterministic fixed-parameter algorithms show that structure helps, but the unrestricted deterministic polynomial-time question remains open.
full_statement: In the Exact Matching problem, the input is a graph $G=(V,E)$, a color or weight function $c:E\to\{0,1\}$, and an integer $k$. The question is whether $G$ has a perfect matching $M$ satisfying $$\sum_{e\in M} c(e)=k.$$ Equivalently, in a red-blue graph, decide whether there is a perfect matching containing exactly $k$ red edges. The problem is in randomized polynomial time by the Mulmuley-Vazirani-Vazirani algebraic isolation framework. The target concerns arbitrary graphs, not only bipartite graphs. The open problem is to give a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary graphs, or to prove a principled barrier showing why such a derandomization would imply a major breakthrough elsewhere. A satisfactory positive solution may derandomize the isolation step, avoid isolation through a different algebraic certificate, or exploit the matching polytope and exact-cardinality constraint in a new way.
known_results:
Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani gave a randomized polynomial-time algorithm via the isolation lemma and algebraic matching computations. The same isolation paradigm underlies many randomized matching algorithms and complexity-theoretic unique-witness reductions. Deterministic algorithms are known for ordinary perfect matching and for several structurally restricted Exact Matching instances. El Maalouly, Steiner, and Wulf gave deterministic FPT algorithms for bipartite graphs parameterized by bipartite independence number. Murakami and Yamaguchi extended deterministic FPT algorithms to more general graphs using odd-cycle-transversal and independence parameters. Fischer, Hartmann, Lendl, and Woeginger show that robust/recoverable assignment variants inherit the unresolved status of Exact Matching. None of these results yields a deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for unrestricted Exact Matching.

2026 claim requiring scrutiny. Yuefeng Du's 'Bipartite Exact Matching in P' (arXiv:2604.01571v3) claims a deterministic algorithm for all bipartite graphs (Theorem 1.1, $O(n^6)$ arithmetic operations, not an $O(n^6)$ bit bound). Appendix A describes only a partial Lean verification, conditional on eight structural hypotheses.

Editorial check. Theorem 2.7(iii) identifies exact-red-count perfect matchings with all vertices of an affine slice of the matching polytope. This identity fails for $K_{2,2}$ with its diagonal edges red and target $k=1$: its two perfect matchings have red counts $2$ and $0$, whereas the slice consists of the fractional matrix whose four entries are $1/2$. Thus the slice has a vertex but there is no exact matching. This refutes that subsidiary identity as stated, not the main algorithmic conclusion. The claimed bipartite resolution is not counted here as an established theorem pending clarification.

Remaining open problem. Give a verified deterministic polynomial-time algorithm for arbitrary graphs. A bipartite-only algorithm, even if verified, would not settle this general-graph target.

progress.summary: Randomized polynomial time and deterministic parameterized results remain established. A 2026 manuscript claims a bipartite algorithm, but a subsidiary polyhedral identity fails on K_{2,2}; the main claim is not accepted here as established progress. General deterministic polynomial time remains open.

counterexample_rationale: The problem asks for an algorithm or derandomization barrier, so a finite counterexample is not the right resolution format. Finite instances can test proposed deterministic algorithms but cannot refute the existence of one.
alphaevolve_rationale: Automated search can look for deterministic isolating weight families, small obstruction patterns for naive derandomizations, or algebraic identities for exact-cardinality matching. A final result needs a proof of polynomial-time correctness or a formal barrier.

literature.synthesis: Exact Matching is close enough to ordinary matching that one expects combinatorial structure, but the exact red-edge constraint blocks direct use of standard augmenting-path algorithms. The randomized MVV approach succeeds by isolating a witness matching and detecting it algebraically; derandomizing this would require deterministic isolation for the relevant family of perfect matchings or a different certificate. Parameterized results show that deterministic algorithms can exploit low independence number or small odd-cycle-transversal structure, while robust assignment reductions show the problem's influence in operations-research models. The unresolved gap is the general graph case with no structural parameter. A 2026 bipartite manuscript is a claim to investigate, not an established improvement in this entry: Theorem 2.7(iii) has the elementary affine-slice counterexample described above, and the Lean development assumes eight structural inputs. Neither the defect in that subsidiary identity nor the incomplete formalization alone proves the main theorem false.

agent_guidance.suitable_approaches: Look for deterministic families of edge weights that isolate every relevant exact-cardinality perfect matching family, or for algebraic certificates that distinguish the coefficient of the red-edge-count generating polynomial without random substitution. Another route is to exploit perfect-matching polytope structure plus exact cardinality through strongly polynomial separation or parity-style decompositions. For negative/barrier work, formalize what class of black-box isolation or polynomial-identity methods cannot derandomize the MVV algorithm.
agent_guidance.verification_notes: A proposed deterministic algorithm must run in polynomial time in $|V|+|E|$ and work for arbitrary graphs, not only bipartite, planar, bounded-treewidth, or bounded-parameter instances. The verifier should test whether the algorithm distinguishes exact red count $k$ rather than merely parity, minimum red count, or existence of some colored matching. If the proof uses isolation, it must show deterministic uniqueness or an equivalent certificate for all inputs. Do not infer integrality after intersecting a matching polytope with an exact-count hyperplane: the K_{2,2} example above disproves this step. For Du's claim, distinguish arithmetic from bit complexity and inspect the eight unformalized structural hypotheses.

where_posed.text: The derandomization gap goes back to Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani's randomized algorithm and is stated explicitly in later Exact Matching papers.
where_posed.quote: Mulmuley, Vazirani, and Vazirani (1987) proposed a randomized polynomial-time algorithm for this problem, and it is still open whether it can be derandomized.
